title: Texas Landowner Biosecurity Checklist: Remote Hog Trap Monitoring
content:
Texas landowners carry a heavier share of both feral hog pressure and heightened biosecurity attention than most states. You already have cattle protocols, extension contacts, and fence maintenance on a list somewhere. What often stays informal is the hog side: which trap sites are active, who reviews them, and whether anyone is watching when a sounder commits at night.

This texas hog monitoring checklist is built for that gap. It is an operations checklist for landowners and trappers, not a veterinary manual. Remote hog trap monitoring is one section among several because trap lines are where unwatched mobile hosts concentrate on Texas ground. For screwworm confirmation and reporting, contact USDA APHIS and your state agricultural extension office. Cameras support observation only.

Texas Hog Monitoring Checklist: Before You Start

Print this framework or drop it into your team chat. Adapt the cadence to your property size, but keep the sequence. Skipping straight to hardware without roles and logs is how trap lines go quiet while cattle checks stay on schedule.

1. Assign ownership

  • Name one person responsible for daily remote trap reviews during alert seasons
  • Name a backup who can send a closure command and log catches
  • Share USDA APHIS and Texas extension reporting contacts with the whole team

2. Map your trap line

  • List every active site: primary baited trap, secondary crossings, shared water edges
  • Note cell coverage quality at each site and last successful camera report
  • Mark which sites pair with commercial systems from hog traps versus homemade panels

3. Set observation rules

  • Cameras observe movement and support trapping; they do not diagnose screwworm
  • Per USDA APHIS, screwworm targets live animals with fresh wounds, not feces
  • Any suspected case in cattle, wildlife, or feral hogs goes to agency reporting first

Weekly Field and Remote Review

Run this cadence every week, more often during active sounder pressure or agency alerts.

  1. Remote health check. Confirm each camera reports, power holds, and night view is readable.
  2. Sounder log update. Site name, estimated count, nights of activity, catch outcome.
  3. Bait and site condition. Review live feed before you drive. Empty bait and flooded pads waste a week.
  4. Closure discipline. Trigger only when the full sounder is inside. Log any partial catch and reset plan.
  5. Wildlife traffic note. Record non-hog activity at bait edges if extension asks for corridor context.

A wild hog trap camera system with live video makes this cadence realistic from the truck or the office. The HogEye steel camera is built for trap-site abuse and the closure decision, not a once-a-day photo ping.

Livestock and Property Biosecurity (Parallel Track)

Hog monitoring does not replace livestock care. Run both tracks:

  • Inspect owned animals for wounds that worsen instead of heal
  • Document handling events that create fresh cuts during high-risk seasons
  • Limit unnecessary vehicle traffic through sensitive corridors when trap sites are active
  • Keep fence gaps and water gaps on the same map as trap sites

Texas properties often overlap cattle, timber, and wildlife leases on the same ground. The checklist only works if hog lines sit on the same map as pastures, not on a separate sticky note.

Remote Hog Trap Monitoring Setup Checklist

When you add or refresh trap-site cameras, walk through install once per site:

  1. Frame inside and outside the trap so you count commitment, not just bait pile motion
  2. Confirm day and night views before you trust catch phase
  3. Protect the mount from hog traffic and gate swing without losing the field of view
  4. Label the site clearly in the app so the right closure command goes to the right gate
  5. Test weak-cell reporting from the actual trap location, not the truck on the road

Trapping Outcomes That Support Biosecurity

Whole-sounder removal lowers the number of wide-ranging, unwatched hosts on Texas ground. That supports biosecurity the same way it supports crop and pasture protection. Partial captures work against both: survivors educate the sounder and often shift to corridors you are not watching.

Remote monitoring ties removal to evidence:

  • You see the catch happen
  • You see whether a new sounder replaces the last one within days
  • You adjust bait and site selection instead of assuming quiet means success

Commercial corral and drop systems integrate with the same workflow. Big Pig drop and panel systems start at $4,499 with HogEye included for operators who want a turnkey trap plus camera pairing.

Reporting and Escalation

Keep this block visible on the checklist:

  • Suspected screwworm in any species: contact USDA APHIS and Texas extension immediately
  • Do not treat or confirm from camera video
  • Log date, location, species if known, and trap-site activity for timeline context
  • Share logs with your veterinarian when livestock and wildlife corridors overlap

Observation at the trap line supports awareness. Agency partners handle confirmation and response.

Monthly Audit (15 Minutes)

Once a month, ask four questions:

  1. Are all active sites still reporting?
  2. Is anyone actually reviewing feeds daily during alert seasons?
  3. Did we log catches and sounder estimates consistently?
  4. Do we need another site on a hot crossing we keep driving to blind?

If the answer to question two is no, fix roles before you buy another camera. Compare pricing and options when you are ready to expand the line.

Texas Trap-Line Scenarios (Quick Reference)

East Texas timber lease. Weak cell in bottoms is common. Test reporting from the trap panel before catch phase. Log which sites need a mid-season reposition versus a booster path change.

Hill Country pasture mix. Cattle and hogs share water gaps. Put the primary texas hog monitoring checklist review on the baited catch site, not only the tank camera facing the road.

South Texas sendero lines. Multiple small traps beat one giant blind spot. Name every site in the app so closure commands do not go to the wrong gate during a fast window.

Panhandle wheat country. Seasonal bait discipline matters as much as camera uptime. A fed trap with a dark unit is still a blind spot. Fix reporting before you add bait.

Onboarding a New Team Member

Walk new trappers through four items on day one: how to open live view, how to read inside versus outside the trap, who may send a closure command, and the USDA APHIS reporting path if livestock or wildlife suspicion arises. Hand them the site map and the weekly log template. Remote hog trap monitoring only scales when the second person can run the checklist without calling the owner at midnight or mid-catch.

Pairing the Checklist With Trap Types

Corral and panel traps need frames that show the gate line and back corner. Drop traps need the full footprint plus approach edges. Net systems need conditioning versus catch phase noted in the log every night. The texas hog monitoring checklist stays the same; only the closure criteria change. Document which commercial system sits at each site if you run Big Pig panels or drop traps from the hog traps catalog so new team members do not confuse sites during a fast window. A one-line note in the log beats a phone call at midnight.

Frequently Asked Questions

What belongs on a texas hog monitoring checklist?

Assign trap-line owners, map active sites, run weekly remote and field reviews, keep livestock biosecurity in parallel, and report suspected screwworm to USDA APHIS instead of diagnosing from cameras.

Can remote hog trap monitoring replace cattle checks?

No. It complements cattle protocols by covering feral hog lines and wildlife corridors where unwatched mobile hosts concentrate.

Does this checklist diagnose screwworm?

No. It is an operations framework. Cameras support observation and trapping. Confirmation and reporting belong to USDA APHIS and your extension office.

How often should Texas landowners review trap cameras remotely?

Daily on active sites during alert seasons, with a weekly sounder log and monthly audit of roles, reporting, and site coverage.

Why include whole-sounder trapping on a biosecurity checklist?

Removing complete sounders lowers unwatched host density and gives you measurable outcomes instead of guessing whether hog pressure changed.
